title: Why Useful AI Products Can Still Be Hard to Adopt

Maya Lee 4 min read · 2 hours ago -- Listen Share In DataSnipper’s product illustration, an AI-generated answer to a loan-agreement question sits beside the passage it cites. The user can inspect the highlighted text, then choose Reject or Approve. The answer is only one part of what the interface has to deliver. Someone still has to decide whether it belongs in the work. Press enter or click to view image in full size An answer, its supporting passage, and a review decision in DataSnipper’s public DocuMine illustration. Vendor-supplied product image; not a test performed for this article. Source: DataSnipper. That is a useful starting point for an AI product team struggling to turn interest into adoption. A convincing demonstration can show that a model finds an answer. It may leave unanswered how a customer gets the right documents into the system, checks the result, and passes it to a colleague who has to rely on it. Each of those steps can add work. To understand resistance, follow the task far enough to see whether the product removes that work, moves it elsewhere, or creates something new. A usable answer needs somewhere to go DataSnipper describes DocuMine as an AI tool for asking questions across documents within Excel. Its public materials show answers connected to source references and a review step in which users approve or reject suggestions. The illustration above makes that connection visible: answer, evidence, decision. Consider the alternative: a separate assistant returns a plausible answer, but the reviewer must reopen the agreement, locate the supporting passage, and recreate the evidence trail in the workbook. This is an illustrative comparison, not a test of a competing product. It shows why improving the answer alone might leave much of the adoption problem untouched. A citation can reduce the effort of finding a passage. It cannot establish that the passage supports the conclusion, that another clause does not qualify it, or that the right document version was supplied. For this kind of product, review remains part of the task. Making review easier is a product benefit in its own right. These are observations about a vendor’s published design, not independent evidence of adoption or retention. The design is worth examining because it identifies a specific burden the product is trying to absorb: carrying evidence from retrieval into a reviewable work product. The task can be difficult to ask for, too There is another burden before the first answer appears. Someone has to turn an assignment into questions the system can use. A blank prompt box leaves that translation to the customer, even when the underlying work is familiar and repeated across a team. In its Question Bank announcement , DataSnipper describes shared, standardized use cases and pre-built question sets. Its illustration offers categories such as IT policy review and lease agreements. Instead of inventing an instruction from scratch, a user can begin with an existing task definition. Press enter or click to view image in full size Question Bank offers starting points for recurring review tasks. The screen shows a product capability; it does not establish that a question set is complete or appropriate for a particular engagement. Source: DataSnipper. The interesting choice is how much responsibility that starting point takes on. A question set can make a task easier to initiate and repeat, but selecting one is not proof that it covers the current engagement. A useful default needs to be easy to inspect and adapt. Otherwise, the product may replace the effort of composing questions with the less visible risk of accepting an incomplete set. That gives the team a more precise research question than whether customers find prompting difficult: where do users spend effort deciding what to ask, and what must they check before reusing a saved set? The answers can shape a feature, a default, or the choice of which customers to serve first. Watch one task cross the boundary For an early-stage team, I would start by watching a relevant user complete one recent task with their current tools. Follow the inputs, the checks, and the handoff. Then attempt a comparable task with the AI product and record each point where the user has to prepare material, restore context, verify an answer, or recreate the result elsewhere. Those observations point to different decisions. Repeatedly rebuilding the same context may justify an integration or saved setup. Being unable to check a conclusion may justify better source navigation. Waiting for data access may require an administrator and a different onboarding path. More prompting guidance will not resolve all three. Some change will still be worth asking for. A new workspace may be justified when the existing workflow is fragmented or cannot support the result customers need. The question is whether the benefit survives the effort of getting there, including work performed by people outside the demonstration. Before adding another capability, identify one point where a useful AI result stops being usable work. Fixing that boundary gives the next trial a concrete question: can the customer now carry a real task through it, with evidence and ownership intact? Sources & image credits DataSnipper — DocuMine .
